title: The first boon granted: the father’s welcome
theme: Yama grants the first boon at once: Auddālaki will know his son again, sleep in peace and be free of anger, seeing him released from the jaws of death.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «यथा बुद्धिः त्वयि पुरस्तात् पूर्वम् आसीत्स्नेहसमन्विता पितुस्तव» — as his affection for you was before

words.meaning: released by me, permitted by me

words.gram: perf. act. participle m. nom. sg.

sandhi.rule: Final t before a voiced consonant becomes d: P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga of -aḥ before a vowel other than a is lost and the hiatus stays: P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि) and P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य).
The visarga after a vowel other than a/ā becomes r before a vowel or a voiced consonant (the ru of P. 8.2.66 ससजुषो रुः, kept as r).
Visarga before t becomes s: P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).

morphology.note: The periphrastic future (luṭ) of bhū, used for a definite future: ‘he will be’.
Periphrastic future of śī ‘lie, sleep’: ‘he will sleep’.
Perfect active participle (kvasu) of dṛś with the connecting i. Raṅgarāmānuja’s text has दृशिवान्, which he explains as a Vedic form without reduplication: «छान्दसो द्विर्वचनाभावः».
A patronymic in -i from Uddālaka; Śaṅkara takes it as Uddālaka himself (the patronymic used of the father) and gives a second possibility, that he was the son of two families: «द्व्यामुष्यायणो वा».

translation.literal: ‘As before, Auddālaki Āruṇi will be recognising [you], released by me; he will sleep the nights happily, free of anger, having seen you released from the mouth of death.’
translation.readable: ‘Your father will know you as before. With my leave, Auddālaki Āruṇi will sleep peacefully through the nights, his anger gone, once he has seen you freed from the jaws of death.’

syntax: Two coordinated future statements with the same subject (Auddālaki Āruṇi): yathā purastād bhavitā pratītaḥ ‘he will be recognising, as before’, and sukhaṃ rātrīḥ śayitā vītamanyuḥ ‘he will sleep happily, free of anger’. The participle dadṛśivān with its object tvām … pramuktam gives the reason. matprasṛṣṭaḥ qualifies the father: he acts by Yama’s leave.

ambiguities.topic: Who is ‘released by me’ — the father or the son?
ambiguities.note: The base text reads matprasṛṣṭaḥ (nominative, with the father): ‘Auddālaki, permitted by me’; Śaṅkara: «मत्प्रसृष्टः मयानुज्ञातः सन्». Raṅgarāmānuja knows a reading with the accusative, which would go with the son: «मत्प्रसृष्टम् इति द्वितीयान्तपाठे मत्प्रेषितं त्वाम् इति योजना» — ‘you, sent back by me’.

ambiguities.topic: Auddālaki: son of Uddālaka, or Uddālaka himself?
ambiguities.note: The patronymic would normally mean ‘son of Uddālaka’, but the person meant is Naciketas’s father, called Vājaśravasa in 1.1.1. Śaṅkara takes it as Uddālaka himself; Raṅgarāmānuja gives both: «उद्दालकस्य अपत्यम्, अरुणस्य गोत्रापत्यं इति वाऽर्थः».

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written the two lines have 22 and 23 syllables; the extra syllable is in the second line (sukhaṃ rātrīḥ śayitā vītamanyus tvāṃ dadṛśivān …), where the Vedic metre allows a hypermetric pāda.

beginner: Naciketas had asked, as his first boon, that his father should be at peace with him again and recognise him when he came home. Yama does not argue; he simply grants it. Your father, he says, will know you as he knew you before. He will sleep well at night, his anger gone, because he will see that you have come back from death. The scene is human before it is philosophical: a son who was given away in anger wants above all to be welcomed home. The Upaniṣad lets the first boon be about family and forgiveness before it turns to heaven and then to the self.
analogy: Like a child who has run away in a quarrel and, before asking anything else, asks only that the door be opened to him again.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The first boon exactly as asked in 1.1.10: the father will recognise the son, sleep in peace and lose his anger, seeing him back from death. Yama speaks in the definite future (bhavitā, śayitā).

commentary.q: Why does the father’s anger matter?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara reads the boon as a return of the father’s former affection: «यथा बुद्धिः त्वयि पुरस्तात् पूर्वम् आसीत्स्नेहसमन्विता पितुस्तव». He glosses the father’s state as one of peace: «सुखं प्रसन्नमनाः शयिता स्वप्ता वीतमन्युः विगतमन्युश्च». Raṅgarāmānuja says the same with ‘by my grace’: «मदनुग्रहादित्यर्थः».

commentary.q: How do the Mādhva commentators place the three boons?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva’s commentary, on 1.1.9, quotes a verse from the work he calls Gatisāra naming the three boons as the father’s good will, Hari in the Nāciketa fire, and Viṣṇu who abides in the freed soul: «सौमनस्यं पितुश्चैव नाचिकेताग्निगं हरिम्». His later commentator Vedeśatīrtha says that this mantra, ‘as before he will be convinced’, is the reply to the first request: «“यथा पुरस्ताद्भविता प्रतीतः” इति परिहारवाक्यं चोक्ततात्पर्यकम्».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: bhavitā and śayitā are periphrastic futures (luṭ), the tense of a definite, appointed future; dadṛśivān is a perfect participle. Raṅgarāmānuja comments on śayitā: «लुट्, सुखनिद्रां प्राप्स्यतीति यावत्».

advaita.text: A plain reading of the narrative: Yama permits the father to be calm and affectionate again, «मत्प्रसृष्टः मयानुज्ञातः सन्». Śaṅkara draws no doctrine from the first boon; it prepares the way for the second and third.

visistadvaita.text: The same plain sense, with Yama’s grace as the cause of the father’s calm: «मदनुग्रहादित्यर्थः». Raṅgarāmānuja notes the alternative reading with the son as the one sent back.

dvaita.who: Madhva (Gatisāra, as he cites it); Vedeśatīrtha
dvaita.text: The first boon is the father’s good will, as the verse Madhva cites puts it: «सौमनस्यं पितुश्चैव». The later Mādhva commentators read this mantra as Yama’s reply to that request, before the boons turn to Hari.

schools.disagreement: There is no disagreement about this verse. The schools differ only in what the three boons together point to: Śaṅkara’s fire and heaven are steps of ritual, the Mādhva reading sees Hari behind the second and third.

parallels.note: The phrase ‘released from the mouth of death’ returns at the end of the first adhyāya, where it is the fruit of knowing the self beyond the senses. Here it is literal, of Naciketas coming home.

contemporary.text: The first thing Naciketas asks is not knowledge or reward but that his angry father should be at peace with him. Many people know that a quarrel at home can outweigh every other success, and that reconciliation can be the most urgent wish. The Upaniṣad places that wish first, and has it granted without conditions. (A modern reflection, not a claim about the text’s purpose.)

reflect.beginner: If you could ask for one relationship to be mended, which would it be?
reflect.deeper: Why might the Upaniṣad grant the human wish first, before the questions about heaven and the self?
reflect.practice: Think of someone with whom you have a misunderstanding. Without deciding anything, wish them a night of untroubled sleep.

references.text: Madhva’s comment on this mantra is not separate in the imported text; his reading of the three boons is in his comment on 1.1.9 (the Gatisāra verse), and Vedeśatīrtha’s remark is there too.

flags.note: Raṅgarāmānuja reports a reading matprasṛṣṭam (accusative) and reads dṛśivān for dadṛśivān; the witnesses of this edition read matprasṛṣṭaḥ and dadṛśivān. The vishvAsa mūla writes vītamanyuḥ tvāṃ with the visarga (spelling only).
